method: Each page was fetched on the date above, converted to text, and read by hand. A figure is 'printed' if the page prints that number for that device and 'derived' if it was computed from printed numbers by the stated rule. Peak figures are vendor theoretical peaks, not measurements.

fp16_dense.as_printed: 312 TFLOPS | 624 TFLOPS* (the page marks only the second value 'With sparsity', so the first is dense; one merged cell spans the PCIe and SXM columns)

fp16_dense.from: FP16 and BFLOAT16 Tensor Core 1,979 teraFLOPS, printed with the mark '* With sparsity'
fp16_dense.rule: dense is half of the sparse figure (NVIDIA's HGX page states this for B200, and the A100 page prints both values 312 and 624)

fp16_dense.rule: dense is half of the sparse figure (NVIDIA's HGX page states this for B200, and the A100 page prints both values 312 and 624)

fp16_dense.from: HGX B200 8-GPU baseboard FP16/BF16 Tensor Core 36 PFLOPS, printed with footnote 2 'Specification in Sparse. Dense is 1/2 sparse spec shown.'

devices.name: Apple M3 (this machine: 10-core GPU, 16 GB)
devices.note: Apple prints no GPU or CPU FLOPS figure for the M3 on its MacBook Air tech specs page or in its 2023-10-30 announcement (https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2023/10/apple-unveils-m3-m3-pro-and-m3-max-the-most-advanced-chips-for-a-personal-computer/), only relative claims such as '65 percent faster than M1 for graphics performance'. This chip's compute roofs therefore come from measurement only.
